title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing -- July 30, 2026
headline: Portugal's face-covering ban cuts its score 5 points, just short of a lower band.
summary: Twenty governments, cities, companies and one university were reviewed overnight, closing a seven-night catch-up run. Nineteen scores were confirmed within the benchmark's five-point range. One proposal moved forward: Portugal's score would fall 5 points after parliament passed a face-covering ban that Amnesty International calls discriminatory, though the finding is held for review rather than applied. A harsher reading would have pushed Portugal into a lower band, but that reading was not adopted because the human-rights case for it rests on a single rights group's statement rather than a court or treaty-body finding. Two entities were flagged tonight for things they did not do. Tacoma was blamed for a detention center that GEO Group, not the city, owns and runs. Fudan University was blamed for a U.S. government decision about it, not anything Fudan did to its own students or staff. Neither score moved. A wildfire lawsuit named the wrong company: Xcel Energy was linked to a Colorado fire that court filings actually blame on a different utility, the second wrong-entity catch in as many nights. Two more checks ran in opposite directions from the usual pattern. Costa Rica's widely reported extradition bill had not actually been filed yet, so it was not scored. A court's dismissal of a discrimination claim against Whole Foods was on a missed deadline, not a decision on the facts, so it was not scored as a point in the company's favor. American Airlines was scored not for a 48-minute outage but for the fact that it was the third time in under two years the same technology failure had grounded every flight. Eleven change proposals now sit in the queue awaiting an editorial decision; none changed a published score tonight.

A harsher reading near 59, which would have crossed into the Functional band, was considered and rejected because the ban's human-rights characterization rests on a single rights-group statement rather than a court or treaty-body finding. topSignals.title: Portugal's Face-Covering Ban Pushes Its Score Toward a Lower Band, but Not Across It
topSignals.whyItMatters: Portugal's parliament banned face coverings in public, and Amnesty International calls the law discriminatory toward Muslim women. The finding cuts 5 points off Portugal's score, but a lower band was not applied because the evidence is not yet strong enough to clear that bar.
topSignals.description: Portugal's parliament passed a ban on face-concealing clothing in public spaces on July 17, 2026, with a two-thirds majority. Fines run from 200 to 4,000 euros, and forcing another person to wear a face veil carries up to three years in prison. The bill originated with the far-right Chega party and was reframed around security and public order in its final text, partly to survive constitutional review. Amnesty International Portugal's executive director said the law "is discriminatory and is a threat to human rights" because it still falls on Muslim women who cover their faces as a religious practice, even after references to Islam were removed from earlier drafts. The finding moves Portugal's score down 5.0 points, concentrated in Empathy, Equity and Boundaries. A harsher reading of the evidence would have pushed Portugal's score to about 59, crossing from the Established band into Functional. That reading was not adopted. Compassion Benchmark requires at least two independent sources, with at least one from a court, treaty body or comparable authority, before a band change is applied on a human-rights characterization. Right now, that characterization rests on one rights organization's statement, with no ruling yet from the Council of Europe or a Portuguese court. The same sourcing bar held back proposed band changes for Microsoft AI on July 25 and Uganda on July 26. Portugal's published score of 65.6 is unchanged while the proposal awaits a decision.

evidence.claim: Amnesty International publicly assessed Portugal's July 2026 face-covering ban as a threat to human rights.

evidence.claim: Portugal's parliament passed the face-covering ban and it drew criticism from rights groups.

evidence.quote: Portugal Parliament approved ban on burkas in public spaces
evidence.claim: Portugal's parliament approved the ban on face coverings in public spaces.

topSignals.title: Two Entities Were Flagged for Things They Did Not Do
topSignals.whyItMatters: Tacoma was blamed for a detention center it does not own or run. Fudan University was blamed for a U.S. government decision about it, not anything it did to its own students or staff. Neither score moved, because the benchmark scores what an institution does to the people it affects, not what happens near it.
topSignals.description: Two entities tonight were surfaced on events that turned out to belong to someone else. Tacoma was flagged over a paused health and safety inspection order at the Northwest ICE Processing Center. That facility is privately owned and operated by GEO Group under a federal contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The State of Washington sued for inspection access, GEO Group refused entry, and a federal appeals panel paused the order between July 21 and 24, 2026. The City of Tacoma is not a party to any of it. Tacoma's own detention-adjacent conduct, an ordinance barring civil immigration enforcement from city property and a fund for detainee phone access, dates to May 2026, outside this review window, and is recorded as background rather than scored. Separately, Fudan University was flagged because the U.S. Department of War added it to a research-security list on July 23, 2026, alongside 130 institutions in China, Russia and Iran. That listing restricts U.S. federally funded researchers from working with Fudan. It says nothing about how Fudan treats its own students, staff or the public. Scoring a foreign government's national-security decision as a mark against the university it targets would be a mistake in kind, not just in degree, so no score moved on it either.

evidence.claim: Tacoma's city council passed Ordinance No. 29105 in May 2026 barring civil immigration enforcement from city property, while city leaders said openly they have no authority over the privately run federal detention facility itself.

The U.S. Department of War's Section 1286 research-security list, which added Fudan University on July 23, 2026, covers 130 institutions across China, Russia and Iran and restricts federally funded U.S. researchers from collaborating with them.

topSignals.title: A Colorado Wildfire Lawsuit Named the Wrong Company
topSignals.whyItMatters: Xcel Energy was flagged for starting a fire that court filings actually blame on a different utility. This is the second wrong-entity catch in as many nights, after Bangalore on July 29, and no score moved on the dropped claim.
topSignals.description: Xcel Energy was surfaced on a report that investigators had identified one of its power lines as an ignition point of the Aspen Acres fire, with a lawsuit filed around July 16, 2026. Two independently dated sources covering that lawsuit were checked directly. Both name San Isabel Electric Association, not Xcel Energy, as the defendant; the allegation concerns a downed power line and uncleared vegetation belonging to that company. Xcel Energy appears in the reporting only in a passing reference to the separate 2021 Marshall Fire. Colorado's Division of Fire Prevention and Control says the Aspen Acres cause remains under investigation. No dated source ties an ignition point to an Xcel asset, so the claim was dropped as a wrong-entity attribution and no score moved on it. For contrast, Xcel Energy did settle the actual Marshall Fire claims: it agreed in September 2025 to pay about $640 million to roughly 4,000 plaintiffs, funded from insurance rather than customer rates, without admitting fault. That settlement remains part of Xcel's standing record. Tonight's -1.9 point difference from Xcel's published score is a grid-rounding artifact, not a new conduct finding.

evidence.claim: Xcel Energy agreed in September 2025 to pay about $640 million to settle Marshall Fire claims from roughly 4,000 plaintiffs, funded by insurance rather than customer rates and without admitting fault -- a different, earlier fire from the one it was wrongly linked to this cycle.

topSignals.title: One Bill Had Not Been Filed Yet; One Court Win Was Not a Vindication
topSignals.whyItMatters: Costa Rica's extradition bill and a court dismissal in a Whole Foods discrimination case both looked, on the surface, like real events to score. Neither was, because one had not been filed yet and the other did not decide anything about what actually happened.
topSignals.description: Costa Rica's president delivered six security bills to the Legislative Assembly on July 27, 2026. The bill making headlines, a constitutional amendment that would widen extradition of Costa Rican citizens to cover money laundering, human trafficking, arms trafficking, contract killing and cybercrime, was not among the texts actually filed, because legislative procedure does not allow constitutional reform in extraordinary sessions. The government said it would file that text on August 3, 2026, after this review window closes. A bill that has not been filed was not scored, and Costa Rica's score is confirmed within a fraction of a point of its published 81.4. Separately, a U.S. federal court dismissed a former Whole Foods worker's discrimination claim on July 24, 2026. The dismissal was on a missed filing deadline, not on the facts of what he described, which included coworkers speaking a language he could not follow in front of him and a supervisor mocking his appearance. Nothing in the dismissal establishes that his account was untrue, so reading it as a point in Whole Foods' favor would have been its own kind of error. Whole Foods was not scored positively on it. The company's real, separate finding this cycle is a two-year-old union dispute in Philadelphia, where Whole Foods contested a certified election result through two rounds of National Labor Relations Board review and lost both times.

evidence.claim: President Laura Fernandez delivered six security bills to Costa Rica's Legislative Assembly on July 27, 2026, but the constitutional amendment widening extradition of Costa Rican citizens was not among the filed texts and is due to be filed on August 3, 2026.
A federal court dismissed a former Whole Foods worker's discrimination claim on July 24, 2026 over a missed filing deadline, not on the merits of his allegations.

Whole Foods workers in Philadelphia voted 130 to 100 to join UFCW Local 1776 in January 2025; the company contested the result through two levels of National Labor Relations Board review and lost both times, most recently in June 2026.

topSignals.title: A 48-Minute Outage Was Not the Finding; the Third Time It Happened Was
topSignals.whyItMatters: American Airlines' nationwide ground stop lasted less than an hour and hurt no one, so it was not scored as harm on its own. What was scored is that this is the third time in under two years the same technology failure has grounded every flight.
topSignals.description: American Airlines halted every departure nationwide for about 48 minutes on the evening of July 28, 2026, after an IT and connectivity failure. No one was injured, and operations were restored within about an hour. Judged as a single event, that is an operational failure, not institutional harm, and it was not scored as harm. What is scoreable is the pattern: this is the third FAA-coordinated ground stop in under two years traced to the same connectivity failure in American Airlines' own systems, after incidents on Christmas Eve 2024 and in June 2025. The airline's own app and website were also unavailable during the disruption, at the exact moment travelers needed them to find out what was happening to their flights. Those two facts, the recurrence and the simultaneous failure of the airline's own passenger channels, are what moved the score down 1.9 points, within the confirmation range.

evidence.claim: Reporting identifies the July 28, 2026 nationwide ground stop as the third FAA-coordinated halt in under two years caused by the same connectivity failure in American Airlines' own operational technology, after incidents on Christmas Eve 2024 and in June 2025.

methodologyNotes.name: The Attribution Rule, Applied to Two More Entities Tonight
methodologyNotes.description: The benchmark scores what a government, city, company or university does to the people it affects, not what happens near it or because of someone else's decision. Tonight this rule applied to Tacoma, where a federal detention center's inspection dispute belongs to GEO Group, the State of Washington, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and a federal appeals panel, none of which is the city, and to Fudan University, where a U.S. government national-security listing describes a decision Washington made about Fudan, not anything Fudan did to its own students, staff or the public. Neither score moved on the flagged event in either case.

methodologyNotes.name: A Rejected Band Crossing: The Two-Source Bar Applied to Portugal
methodologyNotes.description: Portugal's face-covering ban produces a genuine 5.0-point decline, and a harsher reading of the same evidence would cross the score from Established into Functional. That harsher reading was not adopted. The benchmark requires at least two independent sources, with at least one from a court, treaty body, or comparable authority, before a human-rights characterization can move a score across a band line. Right now, the case that the law is discriminatory rests on one rights organization's statement, with no ruling yet from the Council of Europe or a Portuguese court. The same bar held back proposed band changes for Microsoft AI on July 25, 2026 and Uganda on July 26, 2026.

methodologyNotes.name: Anti-False-Positive Discipline Runs in Both Directions
methodologyNotes.description: Most false-positive screening catches evidence that would wrongly lower a score. Tonight two checks ran the other way. Costa Rica's widely reported extradition bill had not actually been filed as of this review, so scoring it would have penalized the country for an act it had not taken. Whole Foods' court dismissal was on a procedural deadline, not a decision on the facts, so reading it as proof the alleged conduct did not happen would have produced an unearned upgrade. Both were declined. A third check, on Xcel Energy, caught a wrongly attributed wildfire lawsuit that named a different company as the actual defendant, the second wrong-entity catch in as many nights, following Bangalore on July 29.

methodologyNotes.name: When an Operational Failure Becomes an Institutional Finding
methodologyNotes.description: A single short outage is not automatically institutional harm. American Airlines' 48-minute nationwide ground stop on July 28, 2026 injured no one and was not scored as harm in itself. What was scored is that the same connectivity failure has now produced three separate nationwide ground stops in under two years, and that the airline's own app and website were unavailable to passengers at the exact moment of the disruption. The threshold question, whether an operational failure counts as a compassion finding at all, was answered narrowly: only the recurrence and the channel failure were scored, not the outage itself.

methodologyNotes.name: Math Hygiene, Referred Rather Than Re-litigated
methodologyNotes.description: Three entities carry a gap between their published composite and a canonical reconstruction from their own published dimensions: Singapore (published 62.2, canonical 63.1), Mauritius (published 60.0, canonical 58.4), and Erie Indemnity, whose composite reconstructs exactly but whose stored band label sits in a gap between documented boundaries. None of these gaps are new conduct findings. All three are referred to a coordinator-level index reconciliation pass rather than re-litigated entity by entity, joining Vanuatu and GEO Group on the same maintenance list.

dailyOpeningQuestion.text: Portugal's proposed reading crosses toward Functional on a single tier-3 Amnesty assessment, the same bar that held Microsoft AI and Uganda's crossings open; would a Council of Europe or Portuguese court finding on the face-covering ban constitute the tier-4 source needed to resolve it?
